lanes.title: Breath, consonants & articulation in sung voice

findings.title: When does a sung tone start?
findings.finding: Measuring the interval between sung vowel onsets and piano-accompaniment onsets across 552 tones from commercial CD recordings by international vocal artists (two experimenters measuring the same piece independently agreed within ±10 ms), the accompanists most commonly synchronised their tones with the singers' VOWEL onsets, not with the consonant that orthographically starts the syllable; lead and lag examples occurred for expressive purposes and varied greatly between songs, being smallest in a fast-tempo song and longest in a slow-tempo song.
findings.implication: The MIDI note-on is a vowel timestamp, not a syllable timestamp: a score-locked pipeline must place the vowel at the note boundary and let the consonant run BEFORE it, and a tool judging a student's timing must detect the vowel onset (not the syllable onset) before it can say 'you were late'.

findings.title: Syllable synchronization and the P-center in Cantonese
findings.finding: 23 Cantonese speakers (13 M, 10 F, mean age 19.1) repeated monosyllables in sync with a metronome at inter-pulse intervals of at least 600 ms; syllable-initial consonant onset preceded the beat by a mean 15.77 ms (SD 37.10; t(22)=-2.038, p=0.054, not significant) while vowel onset FOLLOWED the beat by 74.62 ms (SD 36.75; t(22)=9.738, p<0.05) — a mean C-to-V interval of roughly 90 ms. Manner of articulation dominated the placement (F(6,136)=11.439, p<0.05 for consonant onset): short consonants (stops, glottal stop) began just after the beat while long ones (fricatives, nasals, laterals, affricates) began before it, and the authors note this Cantonese pattern (P-center at syllable onset) contrasts with Germanic languages, Brazilian Portuguese, Spanish and Japanese where the P-center sits at the consonant-vowel transition.
findings.implication: The consonant lead a synthesiser must apply is not a constant — it is roughly the consonant's own duration and it is language-specific, so a fixed pre-note offset (~90 ms) is a starting default that must be scaled per phoneme class and re-derived per language rather than baked in.

findings.title: NHSS: A speech and singing parallel database
findings.finding: Parallel sung and spoken recordings of the same English pop lyrics by the same 10 singers (5 M, 5 F; 100 songs, 7 h) give mean phoneme durations in singing vs speech (ms): vowels 830.5/148.0, glides 486.8/102.8, liquids 479.5/101.4, nasals 586.2/103.5, aspirates 168.0/117.7, fricatives 217.5/116.7, affricates 164.8/120.5, stops 172.4/81.5 — sonorants stretch ~4.7-5.7x when sung while obstruents stretch only ~1.4-2.1x. The same paper reports that Montreal Forced Aligner word-boundary deviation from manual annotation is 25.30 ms for speech but 103.90 ms for singing (inter-annotator deviation 5.70 ms speech / 8.70 ms singing), i.e. the alignment tool degrades ~4x on sung audio.
findings.implication: Duration stretching must be applied per phoneme class, not per phoneme: giving a long note to the whole syllable stretches the /s/ and /t/ along with the vowel and produces the 'robot slurring a consonant' failure — the obstruent should stay near its spoken length and the vowel absorbs the note. And any forced-aligner ground truth used to build a practice companion carries ~100 ms of word-boundary error on sung audio, which is larger than the entire consonant lead in finding 2.

findings.title: MakeDiffSinger — variance-temp-solution: word division and ph_num
findings.finding: The DiffSinger dataset format encodes the vowel-on-the-beat rule directly in its word division: "In singing, vowels, instead of consonants, are used to align with the beginnings of notes. For this reason, each word should start with a vowel/AP/SP, and end with leading consonant(s) of the next word (if there are any)." Breath (AP, 'aspiration') and space (SP) are treated as word-initiating units alongside vowels, i.e. a breath is a first-class scored token with its own duration, not a gap. Repo licence BSD-3-Clause; the DiffSinger engine itself is Apache-2.0.
findings.implication: A permissively licensed, already-shipping local route exists for honouring an existing MIDI line: the score-to-phoneme contract is 'vowel at note start, trailing consonants borrowed from the next word, breath as an explicit token', and the practice companion should adopt the same representation so its analysis and its synthesis speak the same timing grammar.

findings.title: Analysis and Automatic Detection of Breath Sounds in Unaccompanied Singing Voice
findings.finding: Hand-marking 1488 breath events across 29 entries (27 RWC-MDB songs by 16 professional singers plus 2 merged AIST-HDB amateur entries; 15 male, 14 female; 128 minutes total) gave a cumulative breath duration of 438.5 s = 5.7% of all audio. Individual breath events ranged 50 ms to 1225 ms; per-entry means ran from 174.0 ms to 487.4 ms with SDs of 47.7-222.2 ms. Long-term average spectra show a common peak at about 1.6 kHz (male) and 1.7 kHz (female) with secondary peaks at 850 Hz-1 kHz (more prominent in females), and the spectral envelope of a given singer's breaths stays essentially invariant across different songs. An HMM detector on MFCC + delta-MFCC + power reached recall 97.5% / precision 77.7% over 27 songs.
findings.implication: Breath is ~1/18th of a sung performance's duration and has a stable, singer-specific spectral signature — so a singing engine needs a breath model with a per-voice spectrum and a 50-1225 ms duration distribution, and a practice companion can detect breaths cheaply enough (MFCC + power) to score a student's breath placement without a neural model.

findings.title: The effects of breath sounds on the perception of synthetic speech
findings.finding: Across five experiments, listeners transcribed synthesized sentences MORE accurately when a naturally produced breath intake sound preceded them (experiment 1), and this was not a generic acoustic-warning effect: replacing the breath with the spectrally similar sound of rustling leaves produced no improvement (experiment 2), and experiment 5 replicated the benefit with leaf sounds rather than silence as the control. Matching the breath's size to sentence length had no effect (experiment 4), possibly because the sentence-duration range was too small.
findings.implication: The pre-phrase breath is doing perceptual work for the listener, not just filling time, and a spectrally-plausible-but-wrong noise burst will not substitute — so a synthesis pipeline should splice or model real inhalation spectra rather than gate in filtered noise, and stripping breaths from a synthesised line costs measurable intelligibility, not only 'naturalness'.

findings.title: Breathing and Singing: Objective Characterization of Breathing Patterns in Classical Singers
findings.finding: Optoelectronic/pneumotachograph measurement of 7 professional classical singers (2 M aged 39-41; 5 F aged 24-72) and 4 untrained males (21-41) during quiet breathing, a standard song and a free-choice piece found that BOTH groups shortened time of inspiration and raised peak airflow when singing versus quiet breathing. Classical singers additionally used a significantly greater abdominal contribution to lung volume (F(1,9)>28.87, p<0.001) and greater rib-cage/abdomen asynchrony with the abdominal peak occurring before the rib-cage peak (F(1,9)>28.92, p<0.001); principal components accounting for >98% of the variance revealed a consistent pre-phonatory INWARD movement of the abdominal wall in singers that untrained controls did not show.
findings.implication: A sung inhalation is a compressed, high-flow, rhythmically constrained motor event that ends with a posture change before phonation begins — so breath duration in a singing engine should shrink as tempo rises rather than stay a fixed constant, and a practice companion advising a student on breath should target inspiratory time and abdominal set, which are the two things that measurably separate trained from untrained.

findings.title: Vocal tract resonances in singing: the soprano voice
findings.finding: Nine sopranos (5 professionals averaging 12 years of classical training, 4 students averaging 7 years) sang four vowels softly without vibrato while broadband acoustic current injected at the lower lip measured tract resonances directly to a precision of ~11 Hz (reproducibility SD 25 Hz for R1, 60 Hz for R2/R3, 90 Hz for R4). Below the speech value of R1 the resonances stay fixed (e.g. R1 ≈ 420 Hz for /u/ at C4 = 261 Hz); once f0 exceeds it, R1 tracks f0 — at C6 (1046 Hz) R1 and f0 coincided within 20 Hz — with the R1 = f0 line lying inside the data's standard deviations over roughly 600-1000 Hz. Lip-rounded vowels /ɔ/ and /u/ fall below the tuning line near 1 kHz. R3-R5 showed NO tuning (mean |Δf| = 0.24·f0, 0.23·f0, 0.20·f0, i.e. the f0/4 expected from random placement). Consequently, over G5-B5 the four vowels converge and overlap on the (R2,R1) plane to separations comparable with the confusion length.
findings.implication: Above roughly 600 Hz the vowel identity a score requests is physically not the vowel that will be produced: a score-locked engine must apply pitch-dependent vowel modification as a first-class transform (F1 -> f0, with an exception for lip-rounded vowels near 1 kHz), and a diction-scoring tool must stop penalising vowel drift above the singer's R1-crossing pitch because correct technique requires it.

findings.title: Vocal tract resonances in singing: Strategies used by sopranos, altos, tenors, and baritones
findings.finding: Measuring R1 and R2 in 22 classically trained sopranos, altos, tenors and baritones over four vowels across their normal ranges found voice-type-specific tuning: sopranos use R1:f0 over at least part of their upper range for ALL vowels studied, plus R2:2f0 over some of their range and often simultaneously with R1:f0; altos use R1:f0 for vowels with lower speech R1 but can switch to R1:2f0 in the lower part of their range; tenors and baritones generally use R1:2f0 and R1:3f0 over part of their range and various higher-harmonic tunings at low pitch. Singers repeated these tunings with precision, but strategies differed considerably between individuals, especially in the lower voices.
findings.implication: A single soprano-derived formant-tuning rule will be wrong for male voices, whose target is a harmonic of f0 rather than f0 itself — so a singing engine's vowel-modification table and a practice tool's 'is this resonance placed correctly' judgement both have to be keyed on voice type, and the per-individual spread means the tool should calibrate against the specific student rather than a population mean.

findings.title: The Identification of High-pitched Sung Vowels in Sense and Nonsense Words by Professional Singers and Untrained Listeners
findings.finding: High-pitched sung vowels are phonetically underspecified for two independent reasons — F1 is tuned to f0 as pitch rises, and the wide harmonic spacing undersamples the vocal-tract transfer function. Testing the widespread claim that surrounding consonants rescue vowel identification, this study compared identification in sense and nonsense CVC sequences and found the positive context effect DISAPPEARS once the number of legal response choices is equated across conditions: the apparent benefit came from higher response probability, not from phonetic context. A second negative result: professional singers showed no perceptual advantage over untrained listeners in identifying high-pitched sung vowels.
findings.implication: Do not rely on consonant context to carry intelligibility at high pitch — it does not, and this kills the tempting shortcut of 'crisp consonants will make the high notes understandable'. A practice companion must not mark a student down for unintelligible high vowels, and a synthesis pipeline that wants a lyric understood at pitch has to lower the pitch, change the vowel, or accept that the words are gone.

findings.title: Word Intelligibility in Multi-voice Singing: The Influence of Chorus Size
findings.finding: 149 participants identified English words spoken or sung in sync by 1, 4, 8, 16 or 27 members of a high-quality SATB choir. Single-voice recognition exceeded multi-voice recognition in the sung condition, but the difference between four concurrent singers and the full 27 was negligible — intelligibility loss saturates at about four voices. The principal effect of voice density falls specifically on CODA consonants, with plosives /b/, /d/, /g/ and /p/ easily confused and coda liquids /l/, /r/ also a source of confusion; increasing voice density actually FACILITATED the coda nasal /m/.
findings.implication: Word-end consonants, not word-start ones, are where sung intelligibility is lost — so a singing engine's release/coda model (and a practice tool's diction scoring) should weight coda plosives and liquids far above onsets, and any doubling/chorusing effect in the pipeline should be told to keep coda releases coherent because the damage is done by the fourth voice, not the twenty-seventh.

findings.authors: Wu, Hsiao, Yang, Friedman, Jackson, Bruzenak, Liu, Yang
findings.title: DDSP-based Singing Vocoders: A New Subtractive-based Synthesizer and A Comprehensive Evaluation
findings.finding: Training six vocoders on MPop600 Mandarin singing (~3 h per singer, one female and one male, held-out test clips, MOS from 23 and 18 listeners) the authors report that with 3 h of data every vocoder including HiFi-GAN V1 reached MOS of only 2-3, and in a 3-minute-data / 3-hour-training scenario HiFi-GAN collapsed to MOS ≈ 1 ('barely audible', FAD 3.50 female / 10.5 male) while the DDSP vocoders stayed above MOS 2 (SawSing FAD < 1.0). Crucially, SawSing produced an audible buzzing artifact 'notably when singers emphasize the airflow with breathy sounds and for unvoiced consonants such as /s/ and /t/' — redundant harmonics bridging adjacent phonemes — and 'this artifact cannot be reflected in any training loss function (and objective metrics) we considered, so the network fails to take it into account'. Post-processing with Parselmouth voiced/unvoiced flags that zero the harmonic amplitudes on non-voiced portions removed much of it.
findings.implication: The breath-and-sibilant failure mode is INVISIBLE to the metrics a local pipeline would use to pick a vocoder, so consonant/breath quality has to be checked by listening or by an explicit unvoiced-segment measure; and the cheap fix — driving harmonic amplitude to zero on V/UV flags — is a deterministic DSP guard that belongs in the render path rather than being left to the model.

findings.title: Period Singer: Integrating Periodic and Aperiodic Variational Autoencoders for Natural-Sounding End-to-End Singing Voice Synthesis
findings.finding: This end-to-end system states plainly that 'the alignment estimation in singing tasks is challenging because of the presence of breath sounds and diverse variations in pitch', which lets monotonic alignment search produce meaningless score-to-audio mappings; the fix is to constrain the search inside note boundaries. Removing that note-boundary constraint costs CMOS -1.13 in ablation (versus -0.21 for removing the normalizing flow) — by far the largest single term. Final MOS with 20 Mandarin and 19 Korean raters over 20 samples per system: 3.97 ± 0.07 on Opencpop against a 4.24 ± 0.07 recording, and 4.61 ± 0.05 on the internal Korean set against a 4.65 ± 0.05 recording, achieved WITHOUT ground-truth phoneme durations.
findings.implication: Breath is not a cosmetic layer — untagged breath actively corrupts score-to-audio alignment, and the single highest-value architectural decision for honouring an existing MIDI line is to hard-constrain phoneme alignment to note boundaries (worth more than a full point of CMOS) so a breath cannot steal frames from the phonemes on either side of it.

findings.authors: Violeta, Zhang, Shi, Yasuda, Huang, Wu, Toda
findings.title: An Extensive Analysis of the Singing Voice Conversion Challenge 2025 Evaluation Results
findings.finding: Analysing 33 submitted systems, the organisers found top systems reached singer-identity scores comparable to ground-truth samples, but 'modeling the singing style and consequently achieving high naturalness still remains a challenge' — no system reached human-level naturalness, and the named residual difficulty is dynamic information in BREATHY, glissando and vibrato singing styles. They also report that chroma-alignment and speaker-embedding metrics correlate best with subjective scores but are 'still not at a level where it could be considered as a true replacement for subjective scores'.
findings.implication: As of the 2025 challenge, timbre is solved and breath-carried dynamics are not — so a product's differentiator is the non-pitch half of the voice, and its evaluation loop cannot be automated: the aspects that still fail are exactly the aspects the objective metrics cannot see (compare finding 12).

lanes.gaps: Could not find any published measurement of sung-breath PLACEMENT — a distribution of where singers actually inhale relative to bar lines, phrase boundaries or notated rests, with ms offsets; Nakano et al. give breath duration and spectrum but not score-relative position, and Salomoni et al. give respiratory kinematics without score alignment. Could not find a sung equivalent of the Whalen breath-perception experiment: no controlled listening test surfaced measuring whether listeners notice the ABSENCE of breath in synthesised singing, so finding 6's evidence is imported from speech. Could not find a per-phoneme intelligibility or spectral-error breakdown for any modern neural singing vocoder — sibilant and plosive failure is described qualitatively (finding 12) but no paper reported /s/, /ʃ/, /t/, /k/ error rates against ground truth, and the SVCC 2025 analysis reports no consonant-level numbers at all. Finally, the measured consonant lead time in finding 2 comes from a SPOKEN syllable-synchronisation task; Sundberg & Bauer-Huppmann established the vowel-onset rule for singing but their published abstract does not release the ms lead/lag distribution and the full text is paywalled, so no sung-specific lead-time distribution could be retrieved.

lanes.title: Expressive control surfaces — vibrato, dynamics, transitions

findings.title: Measurements of the vibrato rate of ten singers
findings.finding: Sonogram measurement of ten professional singers on commercial CDs, all performing Schubert's Ave Maria: mean vibrato rate across singers 6.0 Hz once the end-of-tone acceleration is excluded; the rate typically INCREASED at the end of each tone by +15% on average, with no typical structure at tone beginnings; within one artist the spread between maximum and minimum rate is about ±8% of that artist's own average. J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 96, 1979-1984.
findings.implication: A vibrato oscillator locked to a constant Hz value is measurably wrong at every note release — the engine needs a per-note rate ramp of roughly +15% into the offset, and a practice tool must score a student's rate against their OWN running average (±8% band), not against a fixed 5-7 Hz textbook window.

findings.title: Vibrato extent and intonation in professional Western lyric singing
findings.finding: Twenty-five tones taken from ten commercial CD recordings of Schubert's Ave Maria, F0 read at every vibrato turning point via a high overtone: mean vibrato extent per tone ranged from ±34 to ±123 cents, with the grand mean across tones and singers at ±71 cents. Extent correlated NEGATIVELY with tone duration and positively with intonation (sharpness); informal measurement of Verdi opera arias gave much higher figures than the Schubert set. J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 102, 616-621.
findings.implication: ±71 cents is the realistic default extent for lyric repertoire — nearly 1.5 semitones peak-to-peak — so a score-locked engine that clamps F0 to ±25 cents of the MIDI note is not conservatively 'in tune', it is structurally incapable of classical vibrato, and a practice tool must widen its pitch-accuracy tolerance in proportion to measured vibrato extent or it will fail every well-trained singer.

findings.title: Vibrato rate and extent in soprano voice: a survey on one century of singing
findings.finding: More than one hundred recordings of the same tone sung by 75 soprano artists spanning the twentieth century: mean vibrato rate fell by -1.8 ± 0.3 Hz per century while extent rose by 56.4 ± 0.3 cents per century; rate and extent are significantly negatively correlated (r = -0.62); rate increase near the end of the tone was reproduced, along with a mean rise in tone pitch, and note duration correlates weakly positively with extent. J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 130, 1683-1688.
findings.implication: Vibrato rate and extent are not independent axes and are not era-neutral — a synthesis control surface that exposes them as two free sliders will let a user dial physically implausible combinations, and any 'correct vibrato' target in a practice tool is period-specific (a 1910 target and a 2010 target differ by roughly 1.8 Hz and half a semitone).

findings.title: Does Vibrato Define Genre or Vice Versa? A Novel Parametric Approach to Vocal Vibrato Analysis
findings.finding: Fifteen professional operatic, musical-theatre and jazz mezzo-sopranos and sopranos each recorded two cross-genre songs plus a vocal exercise; sixteen pitch segments per singer were analysed in Praat (sinusoidal extraction, F0 band-pass, LTAS FFT). The COEFFICIENT OF VARIATION of mean vibrato half-extent — not mean rate or mean extent — was what predictably separated genres, and it was higher for musical-theatre and jazz singers; seven pedagogue judges then classified genre from the samples most representative of each group's average CV, confirming the acoustic result perceptually. The authors state explicitly that averaged vibrato metrics are valid only when vibrato is uniform, consistent, persistent and omnipresent, which is a Western classical opera property.
findings.implication: A practice tool that judges vibrato by mean rate and mean extent is implementing an operatic aesthetic as if it were physiology — variability (CV over the note) has to be a first-class measured parameter with genre-dependent targets, otherwise musical-theatre and jazz students get marked down for correct style.

findings.title: Acoustic characteristics of vibrato onset in singing
findings.finding: First five vibrato cycles analysed for five male singers ranging from a 40-year professional opera baritone to an untrained actor, on held D3 and A3 at mf: vibrato onset excursion RISES into the mean in 81% of productions (Seashore's claim that rising onset is a physiological necessity is only mostly true). First-five-cycle rate ran 4.41-4.86 Hz for the professional versus 7.12 Hz and 7.20 Hz on A3 for the two least-trained voices — the untrained voices had the FASTEST vibrato. The professional's onset excursion on A3 averaged 33.57 Hz of rise into the mean, versus 12.47-19.55 Hz for the trained-student and choral voices, and the time taken for vibrato to settle into a steady cycle was more variable in the less-trained singers.
findings.implication: Vibrato must be synthesised with a rising, settling onset rather than switched on at steady state; and a practice tool cannot treat 'faster vibrato' as 'better vibrato' — in this cohort rate ran inversely to training, so onset shape and settling regularity are the trainable signals, not speed.

findings.title: Sound pressure level and spectral balance linearity and symmetry in the messa di voce of female classical singers
findings.finding: Five trained female classical singers performed 318 messe di voce across their musical F0 range. Change in SPL through the exercise was PREDOMINANTLY NONLINEAR, and the shape of the SPL trace differed greatly between the crescendo and the decrescendo half; SPL range was generally greater during crescendo at higher F0 and during decrescendo at lower F0. Spectral balance (0-2 kHz vs 2-4 kHz) plotted against SPL showed markedly more symmetry than linearity, i.e. the phonation-mode change tracked SPL regardless of direction. The pedagogical assumptions of linearity and symmetry are therefore only half right: symmetric in timbre, not linear in level. J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 121, 1728-1736.
findings.implication: A messa di voce rendered as a linear dB ramp up and its mirror down is measurably not the gesture — the level trajectory is nonlinear and direction-asymmetric while the timbre trajectory is symmetric in SPL, so a dynamics control surface needs an independent level curve and a level-driven (not time-driven) timbre mapping.

findings.title: The rise of fixed pitch systems and the slide of continuous pitch: A note for emotion in music research about portamento
findings.finding: The legato/portamento boundary is a quantified psychoacoustic threshold, not a stylistic label: the glissando threshold of Hart, Collier & Cohen (1990) is G_thr = 0.16/T^2 semitones per second, where T is slide duration. Citing d'Alessandro, Rosset & Rossi (1998) on a 220 Hz complex tone, a 1.5-semitone (150 cent) slide over 50 ms is NOT heard as portamento while a 6-semitone slide over the same 50 ms is, and the same 1.5-semitone slide becomes portamento once the traversal is stretched to 200 ms. Their own F0 analysis of Ella Fitzgerald's c.1958 'Blue Skies' scat measured slides of 25 ST/s over 80 ms, 17 ST/s over 250 ms, -21 ST/s over 200 ms, 12 ST/s over 84 ms and 2.2 ST/s over 490 ms, of which only three cross the threshold; the shortest legato transition measured 30 ms. They also quote Hart et al. that a 10-20 dB amplitude drop over tens of milliseconds — routine at vowel-to-consonant transitions — can entirely obscure F0 changes of up to half an octave.
findings.implication: A pipeline can decide legato versus portamento deterministically from slide duration and interval via G_thr = 0.16/T^2 instead of exposing a vague 'portamento amount' knob, and a practice tool must not flag a fast wide slide as a pitch error — above the threshold it is an intended gesture, and below it the listener cannot hear it at all.

findings.authors: Stasak, Holik, Nguyen, Arias-Vergara, Döllinger, Madill
findings.title: Investigating Automatic Vocal Rise Time Measurement Parameters and Multi-Corpus Vowel Onset Behavior with the Voice Onset Analysis Tool (VOAT)
findings.finding: Four corpora, 146 adult Australian-English-speaking females, manual and automatic vocal rise time (VRT — vibration onset to first peak steady amplitude) per onset type: hard onsets 57.7 ± 48.0 ms and 73.2 ± 40.5 ms; modal onsets 97.6 ± 24.4 ms (n=100 speakers), 61.0 ms and 166.1 ± 59.4 ms across corpora; soft onsets 218.7 ± 120.0 ms and 261.8 ± 70.5 ms. Cross-corpus norms summarise as hard <60 ms, modal 60-160 ms, soft >160 ms. Automatic measurement (Hilbert envelope, 400 ms segment, low smoothing) reached 15.5 ms and 21.3 ms mean absolute error on modal and soft onsets but degraded to 71.0 ms MAE on hard onsets. These are speech onsets, not sung onsets.
findings.implication: Attack type is a time constant with an order of magnitude between hard and soft (roughly 60 ms vs 250 ms), so a singing engine can implement glottal/balanced/aspirated onsets as an explicit amplitude rise-time parameter — but a practice tool that auto-classifies a student's onset must expect ~70 ms of measurement error exactly on the hard onsets that matter clinically.

findings.title: Modelling note's pitch and duration in trained professional singers
findings.finding: Bayesian hierarchical model over the Annotated-VocalSet corpus — 2688 solo files from 20 professional singers (11 male, 9 female, ~7 h, scales, arpeggios, long tones, and 'Row Row Row Your Boat' / 'Dona Nobis Pacem' / 'Caro Mio Ben' sung to a metronome and reference pitch). The average 80% posterior prediction interval was 0.8977 semitones wide for pitch deviation (≈ ±45 cents about the modelled mean) and 0.5698 s wide for duration deviation (≈ ±0.285 s). Named effects: a note's second or later appearance in a piece is sung 11.58 cents FLATTER (95% CrI -16.79 to -6.32 cents); a rest BEFORE a note shifts its pitch 13.56 cents versus only 4.99 cents for a rest after; straight tone deviates -6.25 cents versus molto vibrato -14.82 cents, i.e. straight tone is 8.6 cents more accurate; pitch effect grows 0.61 cents per MIDI number, so ~24 cents at E2 and ~49 cents at G#5; a two-octave interval shifts duration by -12 ms (to next note) and +36 ms (from previous).
findings.implication: These are the tolerance bands a practice tool must ship with: professionals themselves occupy a ~90-cent-wide pitch window and a ~0.57-s-wide duration window against the score, the window is context-dependent (rest-before, repeat, register, technique), and a fixed ±20-cent / ±50-ms grader would fail the reference population it is supposed to model.

findings.title: Synthesizer V Studio User Manual — Note Properties Panel / Parameter Panel
findings.finding: The shipping commercial neural SVS exposes exactly the parametric surface this lane is about, but only in Manual pitch mode. Vibrato: Start 0-1 s (default 0.25 s onset delay), left/right fade 0.02-0.5 s (default 0.2 s), Depth 0-2 semitones peak-to-peak (default 1 semitone = ±50 cents), Freq 1-10 Hz (default 5.5 Hz), Phase -1..+1, Jitter 0-2. Pitch Transition (portamento): Offset ±0.5 s, Duration Left 0-0.5 s (default 0.1 s), Duration Right 0-0.5 s (default 0.07 s), Depth Left/Right ±6 semitones (default 0.15 st). Note Offset ±0.1 s for rubato against the grid. Parameter Panel adds Pitch Deviation ±1200 cents, Vibrato Envelope 0x-2x (default 1x), Loudness -inf to +24 dB, Tension -2..+2, Breathiness -2..+2, Voicing (max = normal, lower = whisper), Gender ±2, Tone Shift ±800 cents, Vocal Mode 0-150%. In the DEFAULT AI 'Sing' mode the entire vibrato surface collapses to one knob, Vibrato Modulation 0.00-2.00 (default 1.00), and switching Manual mode on moves the AI-generated pitch curve out into Pitch Deviation.
findings.implication: This is the reference control surface to copy — its defaults (5.5 Hz, ±50 cents, 0.25 s vibrato delay, 100/70 ms portamento) sit just inside Prame's measured 6.0 Hz and ±71 cents — but note the architecture: the neural pitch model and the parametric surface are mutually exclusive modes, so a score-locked pipeline gets either learned expression OR numeric control of it, never both at once.

findings.title: DiffSinger v2.3.0 release notes (new voicing and tension parameters) + OpenUtau DiffSinger support wiki
findings.finding: The open-source variance-model line names its control surface explicitly. v2.3.0 (11 March 2024) added VOICING, defined as the RMS curve of the harmonic part in dB (successor to the deprecated energy parameter, allowing harmonic power to be raised or lowered in vowels and voiced consonants), and TENSION, tied to the ratio of the base harmonic to full harmonics. Both must be switched on in the model config (`use_voicing_embed: true`, `use_tension_embed: true`) and require the variance model to have been TRAINED with them — they cannot be added to an existing voicebank. The OpenUtau host surfaces these as drawable curves: PITD (pitch), DYN (dynamics), GENC (gender/formant, ±12 semitones over a -100..+100 curve), VELC (vowel head/tail speed, +100 doubles it), ENE, BREC (breathiness), TENC (tension), VOIC (voicing), PEXP (pitch expressiveness, default 100 = maximum), SHFC (tone shift), plus Voice Color. Notably absent from the whole list: any vibrato rate or vibrato extent parameter — vibrato lives inside PITD/PEXP as pitch-curve content.
findings.implication: The open route gives real per-frame control of TIMBRE and DYNAMICS (voicing in dB, tension, breathiness) but hands you vibrato only as raw pitch-curve drawing or as a single 0-100 'expressiveness' dial, so honouring a MIDI line with specified vibrato means synthesising the F0 contour yourself and feeding it as PITD with PEXP turned down.

findings.title: Controllable Singing Voice Synthesis using Phoneme-Level Energy Sequence
findings.finding: The authors state that recent SVS systems reach high audio quality but 'most rely on probabilistic modeling, limiting precise control over attributes such as dynamics', and position their phoneme-level energy conditioning as 'the first attempt enabling user-driven dynamics control in SVS'. Conditioning on a phoneme-level energy sequence (rather than requiring frame-level annotation) cut mean absolute error on the realised energy sequence by over 50% against both the baseline and an energy-predictor model, with no degradation in synthesis quality.
findings.implication: As of late 2025 dynamics — the single most basic expressive axis after pitch — was still a research problem in neural SVS rather than a shipped input, which is the strongest available evidence that a score-locked pipeline needing crescendo/diminuendo control has to either use a system with an explicit energy/voicing input (DiffSinger variance, Synthesizer V Loudness) or post-process.

findings.authors: Zhang, Jiang, Li, Pan, He, Huang, Wang, Zhao
findings.title: TCSinger: Zero-Shot Singing Voice Synthesis with Style Transfer and Multi-Level Style Control
findings.finding: State-of-the-art multi-level style control exposes exactly six singing techniques — mixed voice, falsetto, breathy, vibrato, glissando, pharyngeal — as CATEGORICAL phoneme-level labels; the system does NOT accept a numeric vibrato rate or extent. Trained on ~294 h (GTSinger 36 h / 5 singers, M4Singer 30 h, OpenSinger 85 h, AISHELL-3 85 h speech, PopBuTFy subset 18 h) with 40 unseen singers held out. Technique-control accuracy reached 76.1%, singing-method accuracy 76.1%, emotion 79.9%; MOS-Q 4.05 ± 0.10 and MOS-C (controllability) 4.18 ± 0.08. The underlying GTSinger corpus (Zhang et al., NeurIPS 2024 Spotlight, arXiv:2409.13832) supplies 80.59 h from 20 professional singers in nine languages with phoneme-level annotation of those same six techniques.
findings.implication: A negative result for a MIDI-honouring engine: the best open technique control is a boolean 'vibrato here' tag that lands correctly about three times in four, so a score that specifies 5.8 Hz at ±60 cents from bar 12 beat 3 cannot be expressed to these models at all — technique labels are a style hint, not a control surface.

findings.title: Vibrato Expression Control for Singing Voice Conversion with Improving Independent Control (VibE-SVC2)
findings.finding: Accepted to IEEE Trans. Audio, Speech and Language Processing; submitted 15 June 2026. The system adds independent vibrato RATE control on top of the previous VibE-SVC, which the authors note was 'limited to vibrato extent scaling'. Both controls are dimensionless SCALERS, not acoustic units: extent alpha usable to about 0.0-3.0 (style accuracy degrades beyond ~3.0), rate beta usable 0.1-2.0 (beyond 2.0 the result is 'mechanical vibration rather than a musical expression'), against a stated typical singing vibrato range of 3-9 Hz. An Energy Style Converter is required because conventional conversion 'fails to explicitly decouple' pitch-energy entanglement, leaking residual style into the target speaker representation. Measured: average pitch-style accuracy 0.736 (vibrato-to-straight 0.725, straight-to-vibrato 0.747), zero-shot 0.614, nMOS 4.000 ± 0.077, sMOS 2.932 ± 0.069, SECS 0.785.
findings.implication: Even the 2026 state of the art in independent vibrato control multiplies an existing vibrato rather than specifying one — there is still no inference-time input of the form 'rate = 5.8 Hz, extent = ±60 cents', so any pipeline that must honour a notated vibrato has to generate the F0 contour parametrically (per finding 10/11) and use the neural model only as a timbre renderer.

lanes.licence_notes: GTSinger — the corpus behind TCSinger/TCSinger 2 and the main open source of phoneme-level technique annotation — is released under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (verified in the repository's dataset_license.md: NonCommercial and ShareAlike). That is a hard commercial blocker: it forbids commercial use AND forces derivative works under the same terms, so any model whose weights were trained on GTSinger is unusable in a paid product regardless of the code licence. The code around it is permissive but does not cure the data: AaronZ345/TCSinger2 is MIT, openvpi/DiffSinger is Apache-2.0, nnsvs/nnsvs is MIT, stakira/OpenUtau is MIT (LICENSE.txt), MoonInTheRiver/DiffSinger is MIT. Individual DiffSinger/OpenUtau VOICEBANKS and checkpoints are distributed under their own separate voice-provider terms, which are frequently non-commercial and must be read per bank — the Apache-2.0 on the engine says nothing about them. Synthesizer V Studio (Dreamtonics) is proprietary paid commercial software and its voice databases are separately licensed products; its user manual is usable as a design reference but the product itself cannot be embedded. The M4Singer, OpenSinger and PopBuTFy corpora used in TCSinger's 294 h training mix were NOT licence-verified in this lane — treat as unknown, not as permissive.
lanes.gaps: I could not find a measured DISTRIBUTION of vibrato onset delay (seconds from note onset to first vibrato cycle) over a sizeable cohort of trained singers — Bell & Dobrovolsky characterise onset shape on only five male voices, and Synthesizer V's 0.25 s default appears to be an engineering choice with no cited measurement behind it; genre comparisons (lieder vs opera) are described qualitatively in the literature but I found no resolvable source with the numbers. I could not find any singing-voice-synthesis system, open or commercial-neural, that accepts an ABSOLUTE vibrato specification (rate in Hz plus extent in cents) as an inference-time input — every system located either predicts those internally (Song et al. 2022, arXiv:2211.00996, which models likeliness/rate/depth/phase but exposes none), exposes a relative scaler (VibE-SVC2, Synthesizer V's Sing mode), or exposes only a categorical technique label (TCSinger, TechSinger); the only true numeric surface found is Synthesizer V's Manual mode, which bypasses the neural pitch model entirely. Finally, I could not obtain measured lead/lag values in milliseconds for vowel-onset-versus-beat alignment: Sundberg & Bauer-Huppmann, 'When Does a Sung Tone Start?', J. Voice 21(3):285-293, DOI 10.1016/j.jvoice.2006.01.003, establishes that accompanists synchronise to the singer's VOWEL onset rather than the consonant and that lead/lag scales with tempo, but the numbers are behind a paywall and no citing open-access source reproduced them — so the rubato-against-a-fixed-grid axis in this lane rests on Faghih et al.'s ±0.285 s duration band and Synthesizer V's ±0.1 s Note Offset rather than on a direct measurement of singer-versus-beat asynchrony.

lanes.title: Automatic singing assessment & practice feedback

findings.title: Evaluation Framework for Automatic Singing Transcription
findings.finding: Defines the note-level tolerances the MIR field actually uses, taken from MIREX: a transcribed note has a CORRECT ONSET if it lands within +/-50 ms of the ground-truth onset; CORRECT PITCH if within +/-0.5 semitone (+/-50 cents); CORRECT OFFSET if within max(50 ms, 20% of the ground-truth note duration). Correctness is reported at three strictness levels (COnPOff = onset+pitch+offset, COnP = onset+pitch, COn = onset only) plus named error classes: Only-Bad-Onset, Only-Bad-Pitch, Only-Bad-Offset, Split (one sung note transcribed as several), Merge, spurious, missing. Crucially, the two expert annotators (10 and 7 years of music training, annotating to agreement) were instructed that ornaments -- pitch bending at note starts and VIBRATO -- are NOT separate notes, and that PORTAMENTO between two notes does not create a third note; onsets are placed at the start of the voiced vowel, not the consonant. Corpus: 38 melodies, 1154 s total, all UNTRAINED singers -- 14 children's songs (557 s) from 8 children aged 5-11, 13 pop melodies (315 s) from 8 adult male untrained singers, 11 pop melodies (281 s) from 5 adult female untrained singers (adults from MTG-QBH). Per-note ground-truth pitch is annotated at cents resolution with an explicit per-note tuning deviation.
findings.implication: Adopt these exact windows as the companion's default scoring contract (+/-50 ms onset, +/-50 cents pitch, offset max(50 ms, 20%)), and copy the annotation rule as a SEGMENTATION rule: vibrato and portamento must be absorbed into the note they decorate before any cents error is computed, or a good singer's ornament is scored as a split note plus a pitch error.

findings.title: The Evaluation of Singing Voice Accuracy: A Comparison Between Subjective and Objective Methods
findings.finding: 166 UNTRAINED adult singers (57 men, 109 women) each sang 'Happy Birthday' a cappella; 18 experts (speech therapists specialising in voice, and musicians) rated global pitch accuracy of all 166 takes. Inter-judge agreement: median Spearman r = 0.77 (SD 0.08, p<0.01); downsampling to random subgroups showed THREE judges already give a panel mean correlating above 0.85, so large juries buy little. Mean absolute pitch-interval deviation in cents correlated with the expert panel mean at Spearman r = -0.87 (p<0.01). A three-predictor regression (interval deviation, number of tonality modulations, number of melodic contour errors) explained 81% of the variance in judges' scores (F = 232.17, p<0.001), but only two predictors carried it: interval deviation (beta = .51, t = -6.61, p<0.001) and tonality modulations (beta = -.45, t = -6.33, p<0.001). Melodic contour errors did NOT contribute (beta = .08, t = 1.89, p = .06) -- a null result the authors attribute to their rarity. A 'tonality modulation' is operationally defined as an interval error larger than 100 cents that is NOT followed by a corrective interval of at least 100 cents in the reverse direction. The interval-deviation-to-rating relationship is LOGARITHMIC: judges discriminated finely among accurate singers but barely distinguished slightly inaccurate from very inaccurate performances.
findings.implication: Score a take as mean absolute interval deviation in cents PLUS a count of uncorrected key drifts, and compress the display logarithmically -- a linear cents-to-score mapping over-punishes the struggling singer in exactly the range where real listeners stop discriminating, and under-resolves the range where they do.

findings.title: The Evaluation of Singing Voice Accuracy (self-evaluation sub-analysis)
findings.finding: In the same 166 untrained adult singers, each singer rated their own accuracy immediately after singing. Self-evaluation correlated only r = -0.35 (p<0.01) with the objective interval-deviation measure and r = 0.35 (p<0.01) with the 18-judge panel mean -- i.e. singers account for roughly 12% of the variance in how accurate they actually were. The miscalibration runs in BOTH directions and is asymmetric by skill: 41% of the inaccurate singers (panel score < 4, N = 39) OVERestimated themselves (self-rating > 4), while 63% of the very accurate singers (panel score > 6, N = 84) UNDERvalued themselves (self-rating < 6).
findings.implication: The companion's number will contradict the student's self-image most of the time, and in opposite directions for the two groups it serves: expect to have to justify a low score to a confident weak singer and a high score to a self-doubting strong one, so pair every score with located evidence (which note, how many cents) rather than shipping a bare number.

findings.title: Pitch Perception in Music: Do Scoops Matter?
findings.finding: Across three experiments, 110 participants judged which of two four-tone melodies was more in tune, in a pairwise-comparison paradigm. Stimulus design was calibrated to REAL singing (scoop statistics measured from the Pfordresher & Mantell 2014 corpus): scoops -- the brief pitch transition into or out of a target note -- were synthesised into the initial or final 220 ms of a tone, just under 25% of its total duration, with magnitudes taken from human singers, e.g. 74 cents for an upward starting scoop that preserves melodic continuity versus 58 cents for a downward one; the steady-state 'asymptote' was set in tune or mistuned by +/-50 cents (a quarter tone). Result: intonation judgements were significantly shifted by the scoops alone, F(3,49) = 39.694, p<.001, partial eta-squared = .71, revealing two coexisting mechanisms -- partial statistical averaging of pitch across the whole tone (so a scoop that compensates a mistuned asymptote is PREFERRED) and evaluation of the scoop relative to surrounding melodic context. The authors note scoops are deterministic and goal-directed, not motor noise.
findings.implication: Frame-level cents error is the wrong metric for the first and last ~220 ms of every sung note: real singers routinely deviate 58-74 cents there, listeners integrate rather than penalise it, so score the steady-state portion (or a duration-weighted mean) and treat the transition window separately, or the companion reports a large error where a teacher hears none.

findings.title: The mistuning perception test: A new measurement instrument
findings.finding: Calibration sample N = 333 listeners (227 women, 106 men), aged 18-70 (M = 24.76, SD = 7.95), 185 tested in the lab and 148 online, Gold-MSI musical-training raw scores spanning 7 to 48 (M = 24.21, SD = 10.94). Task: 2-alternative forced choice on 6-12 s excerpts of REAL pop performances (MedleyDB) in which the vocal track was pitch-shifted 10-100 cents in 5-cent steps, sharp and flat, against the unaltered instrumental backing. Measured thresholds: 95% of participant abilities fell in a pitch-shift range of 36.3 to 82.6 cents, with a MEDIAN of 55.0 cents. Musical training moves the threshold but does not abolish it: a low Gold-MSI training raw score of 10 corresponds to a 65.2-cent mistuning-perception threshold, a high raw score of 40 to a 43.2-cent threshold. Test-retest reliability r = .698 (95% CI [.544, .806]) with 30 items, falling to r = .579 with 15. Validation sample N = 66.
findings.implication: The +/-50-cent convention is not arbitrary -- it sits at the median human detection threshold for mistuning in real, accompanied singing -- so flagging errors far below ~40 cents reports deviations the student's own audience cannot hear; the flag threshold should arguably widen for beginners (own threshold ~65 cents) and narrow for trained users.

findings.title: The Evaluation of Vocal Pitch Accuracy: The Case of Operatic Singing Voices
findings.finding: 22 professional musicians (8 women, 14 men, aged 26-73) ranked 14 operatic excerpts sung by 14 different professional or semi-professional singers, using pairwise comparison in a test and a retest. Two judges (numbers 2 and 12) exceeded the chi-squared intra-judge instability threshold (12.592 at 6 df) and were excluded; the remaining 20 showed strong inter-judge reliability (no singer's rank variance exceeded the 14.067 threshold). The method point that matters for scoring: because vibrato was present (mainly on final tones), mean F0 for each note was computed over COMPLETE VIBRATO CYCLES only, and interval size in cents derived from those means -- e.g. a nominal 200-cent interval produced as 150 or 250 cents counts as a 50-cent deviation. A multiple regression on six objective parameters (pitch interval deviation, average tempo, F0 of the starting note, energy distribution, vibrato rate, vibrato extent) explained 78.8% of the variance in judges' ratings (all-interactions model 82.7%), and several significant interaction terms were JUDGE-SPECIFIC: for some judges vibrato rate and extent materially shifted their pitch-accuracy verdict, for others they did not.
findings.implication: For any note carrying vibrato, average F0 over whole vibrato cycles before computing cents error -- and accept that a single scalar 'pitch accuracy' number cannot reproduce expert opinion on a trained voice, because the experts themselves differ in how much vibrato quality feeds their pitch verdict.

findings.title: An automatic singing skill evaluation method for unknown melodies using pitch interval accuracy and vibrato features
findings.finding: Reference-free (no score, no target melody) good/poor classification from two feature families. Pitch interval accuracy: the F0 trajectory is low-pass filtered at 5 Hz, silent sections removed, then matched against a Gaussian comb filter on the 100-cent semitone grid with standard deviation sigma = 16 cents; the sharpness of the resulting long-term offset distribution measures how well the singer sits on ANY semitone grid, independent of key. Vibrato: detected with rate constrained to 5-8 Hz and extent to 30-150 cents, with F0 transitions wider than a 300-cent threshold excluded as note changes rather than vibrato. Data: 600 samples from 12 singers drawn from the 100-subject AIST Humming Database, each singing 50 excerpts of 25 Japanese or English RWC songs after hearing each excerpt five times; the 12 singers were selected as consistently 'good' or consistently 'poor' in a prior human rank-ordering study (Nakano, Goto & Hiraga, ICMPC 2006). Leave-one-out on the combined male-female set: 83.5% average classification rate (precision_good 87.6%, recall_good 78.0%, precision_poor 70.3%, recall_poor 89.0%). Named failure modes: a good singer with NO vibrato is misclassified as poor, and a poor singer with unstable F0 is misread as producing vibrato.
findings.implication: Gives concrete detector bands for the vibrato gate a practice companion needs (5-8 Hz rate, 30-150 cents extent, >300 cents = a real note change, sigma 16 cents around the grid) -- and warns that presence-of-vibrato must never earn scoring credit, because absence of vibrato in a competent singer and instability in an incompetent one are the two errors this feature family makes.

findings.title: A technical framework for automatic perceptual evaluation of singing quality (PESnQ)
findings.finding: 20 recordings, each by a DIFFERENT singer -- 10 singing ABBA's 'I Have A Dream' (2 min), 10 singing 'Edelweiss' -- spanning amateur to professional, split into 120 short utterances. 5 professional-musician judges (Western classical, contemporary, and Chinese-orchestra backgrounds) rated overall quality plus 7 named perceptual parameters (intonation, rhythm consistency, appropriate vibrato, voice quality/timbre, articulation, relative volume, pitch dynamic range) on a 1-5 Likert scale. Human ceiling: average inter-judge Pearson correlation on the overall-quality question was 0.82, with all parameter questions above 0.60. A linear combination of the judges' OWN parameter scores predicted their own overall score at Pearson 0.966 in 10-fold CV -- humans really do compose an overall verdict from parameters -- and intonation correlated 0.910 with the vibrato rating. Machine performance depended sharply on granularity: the best acoustic feature set reached only Pearson 0.59 against human ratings at UTTERANCE level, but 0.904 at SONG level via late fusion (0.725 via early fusion), both p<0.001.
findings.implication: A whole-take score can approach the human inter-judge ceiling, but per-phrase scores from the same features land near 0.59 -- so present phrase-level output as located EVIDENCE (this note, this many cents, this late) and reserve graded quality judgements for the whole take.

findings.title: Assessment of Student Music Performances Using Deep Neural Networks
findings.finding: Florida Bandmasters Association all-state audition recordings, 2013-2015, alto saxophone / Bb clarinet / flute (INSTRUMENTAL wind playing, not sung -- read the transfer to singing with that caveat): 1410 Middle School (grades 7-8) and 1550 Symphonic Band (grades 11-12) technical-exercise performances, expert-graded on Musicality, Note Accuracy, Rhythmic Accuracy and Tone Quality. Best model Pearson correlations with expert ratings: Symphonic Band M 0.744 / N 0.694 / R 0.743 / T 0.649; Middle School M 0.724 / N 0.666 / R 0.630 / T 0.634 (all significant at p<=0.05), beating a hand-crafted-feature SVR baseline (e.g. Symphonic Musicality 0.612). The decisive negative result is cross-proficiency transfer: a Musicality model trained on Middle School and tested on Symphonic Band reached only R2 = 0.193, and the reverse direction R2 = -0.106; for Note Accuracy and Rhythmic Accuracy the cross-category average was R2 = -0.765 -- far WORSE than simply predicting the mean. The paper also states plainly that for this dataset 'the number of judges and the grading rubrics are not available'.
findings.implication: Do not ship one assessment model across skill levels: an accuracy scorer fitted on beginners actively mispredicts advanced performers and vice versa, so the companion needs proficiency-conditioned scoring or per-user calibration -- and discount any published correlation whose ground-truth rater count and rubric are undocumented.

findings.title: Perception of just noticeable time displacement of a tone presented in a metrical sequence at different tempos
findings.id: STL-QPSR (KTH Speech, Music and Hearing) 33(4):97-108; no DOI
findings.finding: 30 listeners of varied musical background (almost all amateurs; one professional musician) adjusted the timing of the FOURTH tone in a six-tone metrical sequence until they heard the sequence as perfectly regular, at constant inter-onset intervals varied from 100 ms to 1000 ms. The average just-noticeable time displacement was about 10 ms for tones shorter than about 240 ms, and about 5% of the duration for longer tones. Subjects' musical training did not appear to affect these values. (The companion study Friberg & Sundberg 1995, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 98(5):2524-2531, DOI:10.1121/1.413218, is widely cited for a smaller 6 ms / 2.5% figure under a different discrimination paradigm; that paper was NOT read primary in this wave and its numbers are not asserted here.)
findings.implication: Sets the honest floor for rhythm feedback: at a 600 ms beat (100 bpm) a listener needs roughly 30 ms of displacement to hear lateness at all, so the standard +/-50 ms MIR onset window is already MORE forgiving than a human ear at moderate tempo and much more forgiving at fast tempo -- a fixed 50 ms window under-reports rushing in slow ballads and over-reports it in fast passages; scale as max(10 ms, 5% of the notated duration).

findings.title: The effect of visual and auditory feedback on adult poor-pitch remediation
findings.finding: Randomised pretest-posttest control-group design. N = 84 recruited (University at Buffalo n=56, Northwestern n=28), 75 retained after inclusion criteria (which required a pitch-discrimination threshold below 100 cents); adults, M age 21.75 (SD 8.02, range 18-70), 84% with no instrumental training and 94% with no singing training. Random assignment to 20 minutes of: visual feedback with auditory doubling (n=25; an iPad app drawing the singer's f0 line against the target), auditory-only feedback (n=23), or an active control imitating foreign-language speech (n=27). Outcome measure: the Seattle Singing Accuracy Protocol, with a sung note counted as an error when it deviated more than 50 CENTS from target. All three groups improved from pre to post. Only the visual group's percent improvement differed from zero, t(24) = 2.55, p = .009; visual vs control was significant, t(46) = 1.8, p = .039, d = 0.49; auditory vs control was NOT, p = .14, d = 0.29. Critically, the one-factor ANOVA across all three conditions was NOT significant and indicated a small effect size. Restricting to participants making at least 20% errors at pretest: visual vs control t(37) = 1.75, p = .044, d = 0.54; auditory improved from zero (p = .041) but still not above control (p = .170, d = 0.36).
findings.implication: Twenty minutes of a real-time pitch line buys about half a standard deviation for adults who start out inaccurate, and nothing detectable for those who do not -- so gate the visual display on measured pretest error rather than showing it to everyone, and do not over-claim: the omnibus test in the best-controlled study of this question was null.

findings.title: The effect of concurrent visual feedback on adult singing accuracy
findings.finding: NULL RESULT over a realistic training horizon. University students NOT majoring in music (adult non-musicians) were randomly assigned to two groups and played the computer game SingingCoach for 10 weeks; the treatment group received concurrent visual feedback on singing accuracy, the control group received none. Both groups improved their pitch-accuracy scores significantly over the 10 weeks, but the treatment group did NOT score significantly higher than the control group. Participants' ratings of their own singing rose significantly in both groups. The authors' own conclusion is that singing MORE OFTEN is what helped, with concurrent feedback adding no detectable increment. CAVEAT ON N: the group sizes are not stated in the publicly accessible abstract and the full text is paywalled, so the participant count could not be verified in this wave. Zhang 2026 (DOI:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1920074) characterises this literature as showing that a group given 10 weeks of concurrent visual feedback performed better during training but converged with controls on a retention test after feedback removal -- classic guidance dependency.
findings.implication: Over 10 weeks the dose that mattered was time-on-task, not the pitch display -- so make sessions-completed the companion's primary success metric, and make any continuous on-screen pitch line fadeable or withdrawn on retention trials, because a feature that only improves performance while it is visible has not taught anything.

findings.title: Acoustic spectral feedback in vocal learning: a systematic review of psychological mechanisms and skill outcomes
findings.finding: Systematic review (OSF-registered, osf.io/qgwxk; CC BY 4.0) of 36 peer-reviewed studies, approximately 2,850 participants in total, individual study N ranging from 1 to 334 with a MEDIAN of only 48; populations span singing learners, music-major vocal students, and beginner-to-professional singers, plus 14 instrumental studies included where the psychological mechanism transfers. The review reports NO pooled effect sizes -- heterogeneity forced narrative synthesis rather than meta-analysis, which is itself the honest state of this evidence base. Two findings a builder must carry: (a) an explicit cognitive-load versus guidance-dependency trade-off, in which real-time spectral displays impose extraneous cognitive load because learners must process both the phonatory action and the constantly changing visual information on screen, with beginners most at risk of overload; (b) a null transfer result -- although one included study's experimental group scored significantly higher on metacognition, F(1,78) = 5.10, p = 0.03, partial eta-squared = 0.06, that metacognitive improvement did NOT significantly predict improvement in singing performance, t = 0.23, p = 0.82. One instrumental study reported performance self-efficacy at d = 0.58.
findings.implication: Design the display for the load budget rather than for information density: show one thing at a time during phonation and move everything else to post-take review -- and do not treat a student who has become better at TALKING about their pitch as one who has become better at singing it, because that transfer measures at essentially zero.

findings.title: The effects of feedback interventions on performance: A historical review, a meta-analysis, and a preliminary feedback intervention theory
findings.finding: Meta-analysis of 607 effect sizes over 23,663 observations (domain-general across task types, NOT music-specific -- treat as a design prior, not a singing result): feedback interventions improved performance on average by d = .41, BUT over one third of feedback interventions DECREASED performance, and this could not be explained by sampling error, by feedback sign (praise vs criticism), or by existing theories. The proposed Feedback Intervention Theory attributes it to locus of attention across three hierarchically ordered levels -- task learning, task motivation, and meta-task/self processes -- with the empirical moderator result that feedback effectiveness DECREASES as attention moves up the hierarchy toward the self and away from the task.
findings.implication: The single most load-bearing design rule for a practice companion: keep every message pointed at the task ('bar 12 beat 3 sat 40 cents flat and entered 90 ms late') and never at the person ('your intonation is weak', skill grades, leaderboards), because self-directed feedback is the mechanism by which more than a third of feedback interventions make performance worse.
