NO LICENCE AT ALL (= all rights reserved by default, not usable): (4) github.com/chitralekha18/PESnQ_APSIPA2017, the feature-extraction code and dataset for the Gupta et al. PESnQ framework in finding 8 -- the GitHub API returns no licence; (5) github.com/biboamy/FBA-Fall19, the score-informed music-performance-assessment code from the Georgia Tech group -- no licence. SAFE FOR COMMERCIAL USE: (6) the Mistuning Perception Test implementation behind finding 5 (github.com/pmcharrison/mpt, Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.1415363) is MIT (package DESCRIPTION: 'License: MIT + file LICENSE'); (7) CREPE pitch tracker (github.com/marl/crepe) MIT; (8) mir_eval (github.com/craffel/mir_eval) MIT -- the reference implementation of the +/-50 ms / +/-50 cents transcription metrics in finding 1, so the scoring contract itself can be built on permissively licensed code; (9) the Gupta et al. APSIPA Transactions ARTICLE is CC BY 4.0 per Cambridge/CrossRef metadata (its preprint PDF carries a stale CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 header) and the Zhang 2026 review is CC BY 4.0 -- but article licences cover text, not the unlicensed code above. NOT VERIFIED THIS WAVE: Smule DAMP (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.2747436), source of 4 of the 5 songs in Gupta et al.'s no-reference study -- Zenodo returned 504s and timeouts on repeated attempts and the terms could not be read; assume research-only until checked.
lanes.gaps: Could not find any automatic SINGING assessment system validated against expert human raters on a sample of TRAINED singers larger than a few dozen: the biggest expert-validated singing sets located were 166 untrained singers with 18 judges (Larrouy-Maestri 2013) and 20 singers with 5 judges (Gupta 2018), while everything at thousands of performances (FBA, 2960 recordings) is instrumental wind playing, and the one large singing set (MAST, 1018 performances) carries only unanimous binary pass/fail labels and a non-commercial licence. Found no study at all that isolates the effect of RHYTHM or timing feedback on singing -- every intervention study located manipulated pitch feedback only -- so the millisecond tolerances in finding 10 come from psychoacoustic discrimination experiments on tone sequences (N=30 listeners) and have never, as far as this search reached, been validated as a pedagogically useful threshold for a singer; nor could any source be found stating what timing tolerance an expert singing teacher actually applies in a lesson. No pooled effect size exists for visual feedback in vocal learning: the 2026 systematic review of 36 studies explicitly declined to meta-analyse because of heterogeneity (median study N = 48), and the retention / guidance-dependency picture rests on a handful of paywalled studies. Finally, no source was found giving a measured cents or millisecond threshold at which a practice tool's feedback becomes DISCOURAGING -- the strongest evidence on that question (Kluger & DeNisi) is domain-general and thirty years old -- and two secondary summaries encountered during this wave DISAGREED about whether Wilson, Lee, Callaghan & Thorpe (2008, Journal of Interdisciplinary Music Studies 2(1&2):157-172) found that real-time visual feedback HARMED skilled singers through added cognitive load; the primary could not be retrieved, so that claim is deliberately excluded from the findings above rather than repeated.

lanes.title: Singing-voice datasets, provenance & licences

findings.title: VocalSet: A Singing Voice Dataset
findings.finding: 10.1 hours, 20 professional singers (11 male, 9 female per the ISMIR paper), English, a cappella, 17 vocal techniques demonstrated on 5 vowels across scales, arpeggios, long tones and excerpts; 44.1 kHz. NO score, MIDI, or phoneme annotation of any kind - technique and singer labels only, encoded in the file naming. Exact licence: CC BY 4.0. Verified through DataCite DOI metadata for 10.5281/zenodo.1193957, whose rightsList reads 'Creative Commons Attribution 4.0' with rightsUri https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0; independently mirrored by OpenAIRE as 'CC BY'. COMMERCIAL USE: YES, attribution only. CAVEAT worth recording: zenodo.org returned HTTP 504 to every request from this rig on 2026-09-09 (web UI and REST API alike), so the record page could not be read directly; and the CC BY 4.0 notice in the footer of the ISMIR 2018 paper is the standard ISMIR PAPER licence, not the dataset licence - citing it as the dataset licence is a common conflation and is not evidence.
findings.implication: This is the one substantial English singing corpus the studio can train on and ship commercially, but with no score or phoneme alignment it supports timbre, technique and singer-identity work only, not score-conditioned synthesis.

findings.title: PJS: phoneme-balanced Japanese singing voice corpus
findings.finding: 27.20 minutes of singing plus 12.09 minutes of parallel speech on the same texts; 1 singer; Japanese; 100 short songs. 48 kHz / 24-bit WAV. Ships MIDI, MusicXML, phoneme labels, and per-song composition notes (genre, scale) - full score-plus-phoneme annotation. Exact licence: CC BY-SA 4.0, applied to ALL data in the corpus (verified by fetching the project page HTML directly; the paper repeats it and states the corpus is available for both research and commercial use, explicitly contrasting itself with the NC corpora). COMMERCIAL USE: YES, with attribution and ShareAlike. The copyright cleanliness is structural, not incidental: the first author composed all 100 melodies himself over the phoneme-balanced Voice Actress Corpus sentences, so no third-party musical work is embedded. Two honest limits: the singer is the composer, a non-professional Japanese male in his twenties, and recording was in a simple quiet room at 15 cm mic distance, not a professional studio.
findings.implication: The only corpus found in this lane that is simultaneously commercially licensed AND score-plus-phoneme annotated - it is the correct legal template for building our own, but at 27 minutes of one amateur Japanese voice it is a pilot corpus, not a training set.

findings.title: JVS-MuSiC: Japanese multispeaker singing-voice corpus
findings.finding: THE MOST DANGEROUS ENTRY IN THIS LANE - it is widely cited as CC BY-SA 4.0 and that is false for the audio. Raw page HTML retrieved and grepped directly: the CC BY-SA 4.0 grant covers the TAGS only (singer similarity, key, tempo). The audio data and Melodyne project files are separately restricted to academic research, non-commercial research including inside commercial organisations, and personal use; redistribution is not permitted, beyond posting roughly three sample files. A paid higher-quality 48 kHz / 24-bit version is offered by contacting the maintainers, which confirms the free tier is deliberately non-commercial. Contents: 100 singers (whose speech is in the JVS corpus), 2 songs each, ~2.3 hours, Japanese, 24 kHz studio recording; the common song is the children's song Katatsumuri. No phoneme or score annotation. COMMERCIAL USE: NO. Corroborating evidence that the field gets this wrong: the expert survey table in Shi et al. (Interspeech 2024, Table 1) lists JVS-MuSiC's licence as plain 'CC'.
findings.implication: Blocked - and it is the exact failure mode this studio's provenance rule exists to catch, because an SPDX-style tag scraped from a citation would have passed it as permissive when the audio itself is non-commercial and non-redistributable.

findings.authors: Zhang, Lichao; Li, Ruiqi; Wang, Shoutong; Deng, Liqun; Liu, Jinglin; Ren, Yi; He, Jinzheng; Huang, Rongjie; Zhu, Jieming; Chen, Xiao; Zhao, Zhou (Zhejiang University / Huawei Noah's Ark Lab)
findings.title: M4Singer: A Multi-Style, Multi-Singer and Musical Score Provided Mandarin Singing Corpus
findings.finding: 29.8 hours, 20 professional singers covering all four SATB types, Mandarin, 700 Chinese pop songs. Manually composed musical scores for every recorded song plus manual phoneme alignment (coarse batch script then manual fine annotation). Exact licence, read from dataset_license.md at source: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, with the NonCommercial term called out explicitly in the file. The agreement adds non-CC terms on top: the user must defend and indemnify the M4Singer authors against claims arising from use, must warrant authority to bind their employer, and must cite the paper. Distribution is a Google Drive link, and downloading is deemed acceptance. COMMERCIAL USE: NO.
findings.implication: Blocked for anything we ship; the added indemnity clause makes it worse than a bare CC BY-NC-SA, since it imports contractual liability on top of the copyright restriction.

findings.authors: Wang, Y.; Wang, X.; Zhu, P.; Wu, J.; et al. (NPU / NetEase Tianyin)
findings.title: Opencpop: A High-Quality Open Source Chinese Popular Song Corpus for Singing Voice Synthesis
findings.finding: 5.2 hours, 1 professional female singer, Mandarin, 100 songs, 44.1 kHz, with phoneme boundary annotation and note/score annotation - it is the reference Mandarin SVS corpus. Exact licence, read from the project's own licence page: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. The ND is the decisive term and is almost universally dropped when Opencpop is cited: NoDerivatives withholds permission to distribute adapted material at all, which reaches a segmented or re-annotated redistribution of the corpus and is at minimum unresolved for a model trained on it - and it bites even for non-commercial use, where the NC term alone would not. Independently corroborated by Shi et al. (Interspeech 2024) Table 1, which lists Opencpop as CC-NC-ND. Commercial licensing is available by email to the Opencpop team (address on their licence page), and copyright stays with them. COMMERCIAL USE: NO by default.
findings.implication: Blocked twice over; if we ever wanted Mandarin score-conditioned data the only lawful route is negotiating a direct licence with the Opencpop team, not relying on the public terms.

findings.authors: Zhang, Yu; Pan, Changhao; Guo, Wenxiang; et al. (Zhejiang University)
findings.title: GTSinger: A Global Multi-Technique Singing Corpus with Realistic Music Scores for All Singing Tasks
findings.finding: The best-annotated open singing corpus: 80.59 hours, 20 professional singers, 9 languages (Chinese, English, Japanese, Korean, Russian, Spanish, French, German, Italian), 1,366 songs, 48 kHz / 24-bit, plus 16.16 hours of paired speech. Annotation is manual phoneme-to-audio alignment in Praat, six technique labels (mixed voice, falsetto, breathy, pharyngeal, vibrato, glissando), global style labels (method, emotion, range, pace), and realistic MusicXML scores. Exact licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, stated in the paper and in dataset_license.md. COMMERCIAL USE: NO. TWO DEFECTS FOUND AT THE DISTRIBUTION SURFACE: (a) the Hugging Face repo GTSinger/GTSinger, which is the download route named in the paper and has 20,194 downloads, declares NO licence at all - the HF API returns cardData.license null and no license: tag, so the file people actually pull is unlabelled; (b) the text of GTSinger's own dataset_license.md indemnifies 'the authors of M4Singer', i.e. it is a copy-paste of the M4Singer agreement with the dataset name left unchanged.
findings.implication: Blocked commercially, and a caution for our own publishing: the licence a paper states and the licence its download surface declares are different artifacts, and only the latter travels with the files.

findings.authors: Choi, Soonbeom; Kim, Wonil; Park, Saebyul; Yong, Sangeon; Nam, Juhan (KAIST)
findings.title: CSD: Children's Song Dataset for Singing Voice Research
findings.finding: 100 songs (50 Korean, 50 English) sung by 1 Korean female professional pop singer, each recorded in two keys for 200 recordings, roughly 4.6 hours. Every recording is paired with a monophonic MIDI transcription whose note onsets and offsets were manually fine-tuned against the syllable, plus grapheme-level and phoneme-level lyric annotation (IPA-based romanised symbols). Exact licence: cc-by-nc-sa-4.0, and this one is machine-verified to SPDX grade - the DataCite record for the DOI carries rightsIdentifier 'cc-by-nc-sa-4.0' with rightsIdentifierScheme 'SPDX' and rightsUri pointing at the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 legalcode. The GitHub README repeats it and states the dataset is prohibited from commercial use. COMMERCIAL USE: NO.
findings.implication: Blocked - which is a real loss, because its manually fine-tuned note boundaries and bilingual KO/EN pairing make it the cleanest small score-aligned corpus in the set.

findings.authors: Huang, Rongjie; Chen, Feiyang; Ren, Yi; Liu, Jinglin; Cui, Chenye; Zhao, Zhou (Zhejiang University)
findings.title: OpenSinger (released with Multi-Singer: Fast Multi-Singer Singing Voice Vocoder With A Large-Scale Corpus)
findings.finding: 50 hours of professional-studio Chinese pop singing, 24 kHz / 16-bit; the released set is 66 singers (30 hours from 41 females, 20 hours from 25 males) over 1,146 songs, against 93 singers described as collected in the paper - a discrepancy the release does not explain. No score, MIDI, or phoneme annotation: the Shi et al. survey marks it usable for singing voice conversion but not score-based synthesis. Exact licence as stated on the release page: CC BY-NC-SA 2.0 - note the version, 2.0 and not 4.0, which is an unusual pin for a 2021 dataset and means the older, jurisdiction-flavoured CC generation applies. Access is by application, then a Google Drive share link; downloading is deemed acceptance. COMMERCIAL USE: NO.
findings.implication: Blocked; and if it ever mattered, the 2.0 pin would have to be read on its own terms rather than assumed equivalent to the 4.0 text everyone actually knows.

findings.authors: Sharma, Bidisha; Gao, Xiaoxue; Vijayan, Karthika; Tian, Xiaohai; Li, Haizhou (NUS HLT Lab)
findings.title: NHSS: A speech and singing parallel database
findings.finding: 100 English pop songs sung and spoken by 10 singers (5 male, 5 female), 7 hours total of which roughly 4.8 hours is sung, with manual utterance-level and word-level annotation only - no phoneme alignment, no MIDI, no score. There is NO standard licence. The full EULA PDF was retrieved and its text extracted: it is a bespoke NUS End User License Agreement (04/2020) which self-describes as an Open Source License while being the opposite of one. Terms: use requires the End User to SIGN the agreement and email the PDF to haizhou.li@nus.edu.sg before any access; the grant is internal, non-commercial, scientific-research-only, non-exclusive and non-transferable. Section 9 bans commercial use and names testing commercial systems and proving the efficiency of commercial systems as prohibited examples. Section 6 imposes a copyleft duty: any derivative work, product, service or improvement must be left freely available to other End Users and a copy of any modification submitted back to NUS. Section 7 bans redistribution without prior authorisation. Section 10 states that small portions cannot be used in any publication. Section 8 defines the research scope as testing algorithms for audio-only, video-only and audio-visual speaker localization and tracking - which has nothing to do with a speech-and-singing corpus and is a copy-paste artifact from an unrelated audio-visual EULA. COMMERCIAL USE: NO, and section 6 would additionally force publication of any model derived from it.
findings.implication: Blocked, and the strongest single illustration in this lane that the phrase 'Open Source License' printed on a document is not a licence identifier - it is a signature-gated, non-commercial, copyleft-on-derivatives research contract under Singapore law.

findings.authors: Duan, Zhiyan; Fang, Haotian; Li, Bo; Sim, Khe Chai; Wang, Ye (NUS Sound and Music Computing Lab)
findings.title: The NUS Sung and Spoken Lyrics Corpus (NUS-48E): A Quantitative Comparison of Singing and Speech
findings.finding: NEGATIVE RESULT - the field's default English singing benchmark has NO LOCATABLE LICENCE. Contents: 48 recordings of 20 unique English songs, 12 subjects of varying accent and musical background, 169 minutes of sung plus spoken material of which roughly 1.9 hours is sung, with complete transcription and phone-level duration annotation covering 25,474 phone instances - genuinely good annotation for its era. Distribution: the SMC-NUS lab page links a bare public Google Drive folder named nus-smc-corpus_48. Probed on 2026-09-09: the link resolves HTTP 200 and the folder title renders without authentication, so the corpus IS still downloadable. What does not exist anywhere - not on the lab page, not beside the Drive link, not in the paper - is any licence, terms of use, agreement, or contact procedure. Shi et al. (Interspeech 2024) Table 1 classifies it 'Research-only', but that classification is the survey authors' inference; it appears nowhere in the distribution itself. COMMERCIAL USE: unresolved, and therefore no.
findings.implication: Disqualified under this studio's rule: freely downloadable is not licensed, silence is not permission, and a decade of papers training on it does not create a grant we can rely on.

findings.authors: Ogawa, Itsuki; Morise, Masanori (Meiji University); singer Himika Akaneya
findings.title: Tohoku Kiritan singing database: A singing database for statistical parametric singing synthesis using Japanese pop songs
findings.finding: NEGATIVE RESULT of a different kind - there is no licence because there is no licensor grant; the corpus rides a statutory exception. 50 J-pop songs, roughly 1 hour, 1 professional singer (Himika Akaneya, the Tohoku Kiritan voice provider), studio recorded, with manually labelled phoneme boundaries and MusicXML/MIDI score data. The songs are third-party copyrighted J-pop. The paper states outright that release was made possible by the 2019 amendment to Article 30-4 of Japan's Copyright Act, the information-analysis carve-out, which permits exploiting a work where it is not a person's purpose to personally enjoy or cause another person to enjoy what the work expresses. Access is gated: users electronically sign a letter of intent on a website (zunko.jp/kiridev/login.php) certifying use within that purpose; the audio is behind that login and only the label data sits on GitHub, which repeats that use is limited to the scope of amended Article 30-4. Shi et al. classify it 'Research-only'. COMMERCIAL USE: NO.
findings.implication: Blocked, and structurally unfixable for us: a Japanese TDM exception is jurisdiction-bound and does not travel with a shipped artifact, and synthesising a voice for listeners to enjoy is precisely the purpose Article 30-4 carves out of its own permission.

findings.authors: Shi, Lin, Bai, Zhang, Wu, Tang, Yu, Jin, Watanabe (CMU / Duke Kunshan / RUC) — and separately Gu, Wang, Zhang, Zhang, Fang, He, Wu (CUHK-Shenzhen)
findings.title: The two routes past the 50-hour ceiling: ACE-Opencpop / ACE-KiSing (synthetic) and SingNet (scraped)
findings.finding: Both large-scale escapes from the ~50-hour ceiling fail provenance, in opposite ways. (A) ACE-Opencpop 128.9 hours / 30 vocalists (Mandarin) and ACE-KiSing 32.5 hours / 34 vocalists (CN+EN), with full score and phoneme alignment, on Hugging Face as espnet/ace-opencpop-segments and espnet/kising-v2-segments. Exact licence: CC-BY-NC-4.0. But the audio is WHOLLY SYNTHETIC - rendered in ACE Studio, a commercial singing synthesiser, with manual F0, vibrato, breath and duration tuning, over the song lists of Opencpop and KiSing. The authors append their own caution that using singing voices from commercial software as SVS training data raises legal and ethical issues. The chain compounds: the source Opencpop is CC BY-NC-ND (no derivatives), and ACE Studio's virtual singers are themselves built from separately-contracted real voice providers. (B) SingNet, arXiv:2505.09325, 14 May 2025, 3,000 hours - 2,629 hours source-separated with MDX23 from in-the-wild songs sourced from online music streaming platforms, plus 321 hours from commercial sample packs. The paper carries NO licence statement, NO copyright section and NO ethics statement; only the checkpoints (Wav2vec2, BigVGAN, NSF-HiFiGAN) are described as open-sourced, not the audio; and the advertised project page singnet-dataset.github.io returned HTTP 404 on 2026-09-09. COMMERCIAL USE: NO for ACE; unresolved-and-therefore-no for SingNet.
findings.implication: The largest corpora in the literature are the least usable: one is a licence chain through a commercial synthesiser we have not licensed, the other is separated vocals from commercial recordings with no provenance at all.

findings.authors: Zhang, Yu; Pan, Changhao; Guo, Wenxiang; et al. (Zhejiang University)
findings.title: GTSinger cost disclosure — what a from-scratch annotated singing corpus actually costs
findings.finding: GTSinger is the rare dataset paper that discloses its actual spend, giving a hard build-cost anchor. RECORDING: professional singers hired at USD 300 per hour of audio recorded, USD 30,000 total. Conditions: professional studio, singers monitoring the song's accompaniment on headphones so vocals come out clean but rhythmically locked, 48 kHz / 24-bit WAV. ANNOTATION: experts with music and language backgrounds hired at USD 15 per hour for phoneme-level alignment correction in Praat, six-way technique labelling, global style labelling and MusicXML score composition with expert review; USD 18,000 total. TOTALS: USD 48,000 for 80.59 finished hours, about USD 596 per annotated hour, split roughly USD 372/hour recording and USD 223/hour annotation. Reading the annotation figure against the USD 15 rate implies on the order of 15 expert-hours of labour per hour of audio, i.e. roughly a 15:1 annotation-to-audio ratio, or about 15 minutes of expert work per minute of singing. Note this excludes studio hire, engineering, and the singers' own rehearsal time, so it is a floor.
findings.implication: A 10-hour commercially-clean corpus of our own is a ~USD 6,000 / ~150 expert-hour project at these rates - genuinely affordable at studio scale, and the only route that clears every licence problem in this lane at once.

findings.authors: Cotton, Holzapfel, de Vries, Berglund, Tatar
findings.title: Revising research practices for singing data collection — and the 2024-2026 voice-replica statutes
findings.finding: Peer-reviewed and open access (CC BY 4.0) in AI & SOCIETY, 12 July 2026. Applying the Ethically Aligned Stakeholder Elicitation (EASE) framework to three singing datasets, the authors show that singers who contribute data hold consistently lower power than the researchers who collect it: the contribution is event-centric, a one-off recording session, which structurally excludes contributors from the licensing and access decisions made afterwards, while it is contributors and not collectors who bear the harm from non-consensual downstream use such as vocal deepfakes. The statutory picture behind that argument, as of 2026-09-09: Tennessee's ELVIS Act took effect 1 July 2024, was the first US law to make voice itself a protected property right covering both actual voice and simulations of it, and critically reaches the distribution of a technology whose primary purpose is producing a particular identifiable individual's voice - a knowledge standard applies, remedies are civil plus Class A misdemeanour, and labels holding exclusive rights can sue on an artist's behalf. California AB 1836 (deceased performers' digital replicas, effective 1 January 2026) and AB 2602 (contractual consent for living performers) were signed 17 September 2024. Federally, the NO FAKES Act of 2026 (S.4591) was introduced 20 May 2026, advanced unanimously out of Senate Judiciary on 18 June 2026 and was placed on the Senate calendar on 24 June 2026; it would create a licensable federal property right in voice and likeness with a DMCA-style notice-and-takedown regime, First Amendment carve-outs for news, parody and criticism, and a non-commercial research exemption limited to nonprofit libraries, archives and accredited nonprofit educational institutions - which a commercial studio is not.
findings.implication: Cloning a named singer requires that singer's written, use-scoped consent, not a dataset licence: the ELVIS Act already reaches the act of distributing a model built to produce one identifiable person's voice, and NO FAKES would make that a federal right whose research exemption we do not qualify for.

lanes.licence_notes: COMMERCIALLY USABLE — 2 of the 13 corpora examined. VocalSet (CC BY 4.0, verified in DataCite rightsList; 10.1 h English, technique-rich, but zero score or phoneme annotation) and PJS (CC BY-SA 4.0 on all data, explicitly commercial-permitted; 27 minutes of one amateur Japanese voice, but with MIDI, MusicXML and phoneme labels, and copyright-clean by construction because the author composed the songs). Note PJS's ShareAlike: derivative DATASETS inherit CC BY-SA 4.0, so a corpus we build on top of it is encumbered even though a shipped model is arguably not. NON-COMMERCIAL BY EXPLICIT LICENCE — 6: M4Singer (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, plus an indemnity clause), GTSinger (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), CSD (cc-by-nc-sa-4.0, SPDX-confirmed via DataCite), OpenSinger (CC BY-NC-SA 2.0 — version 2.0, not 4.0), ACE-Opencpop and ACE-KiSing (CC-BY-NC-4.0). NON-COMMERCIAL PLUS NO-DERIVATIVES — 1: Opencpop is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, and the ND term is routinely dropped when it is cited; it withholds distribution of adapted material even for non-commercial users, which reaches re-segmented or re-annotated redistributions and is unresolved for trained models. MISLABELLED IN THE WILD — 1, and it is the most important line here: JVS-MuSiC is cited everywhere as CC BY-SA 4.0, but reading the terms page shows that grant covers the TAGS only, while the audio is academic/non-commercial/personal use with redistribution prohibited. The expert survey table in Shi et al. (Interspeech 2024) records it as 'CC', so this error is present in the literature, not just in blog posts. NO LOCATABLE LICENCE AT ALL — 3, every one disqualifying: NUS-48E ships from a bare public Google Drive folder (confirmed live, HTTP 200, no auth) with no terms stated anywhere; SingNet's 3,000 hours have no licence, no copyright section and no ethics statement, and its project page 404s; and GTSinger's Hugging Face repo — the download route the paper names, with 20,194 downloads — declares no licence in its metadata at all, even though the paper and the GitHub file both say CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. SIGNED AGREEMENT REQUIRED — 2: NHSS demands a signed EULA emailed to a named NUS professor before access, and Kiritan requires an electronic letter of intent on a login-gated site. NEITHER A LICENCE NOR A STANDARD ONE — NHSS's document calls itself an 'Open Source License' while being a signature-gated, non-commercial, copyleft-on-derivatives, no-redistribution research contract under Singapore law (its scope clause even describes audio-visual speaker localization, a copy-paste from an unrelated EULA); Kiritan has no licence and instead rides Article 30-4 of Japan's Copyright Act, a jurisdiction-bound information-analysis exception that expressly does not cover use where the purpose is for someone to enjoy the work. Two further hygiene findings: GTSinger's dataset_license.md indemnifies 'the authors of M4Singer', i.e. it was copied without editing; and the CC BY 4.0 in the ISMIR paper footer covers the PAPER, so it is not evidence of any dataset's licence. BOTTOM LINE: no open singing corpus with score and phoneme annotation at usable scale is commercially licensed. The only clean path to a shippable model line is recording our own, and GTSinger's disclosed spend prices that at roughly USD 596 per finished annotated hour (USD 300/audio-hour for professional singers, ~USD 223/audio-hour for annotation at USD 15/hour, i.e. about a 15:1 expert-hour-to-audio-hour ratio).
lanes.gaps: Could not read zenodo.org at all — every request from this rig on 2026-09-09 returned HTTP 504 from the web UI and the REST API alike, so VocalSet's and CSD's licences were established through DataCite DOI metadata and OpenAIRE rather than the record pages themselves; DataCite gave CSD an explicit SPDX identifier but gave VocalSet only the CC BY 4.0 name and URI without a version-pinned SPDX tag, so 'CC BY 4.0' rests on the rightsUri, not on an SPDX string. Could not resolve several things I looked for specifically: whether SingNet's audio was ever released and under what terms (the project page 404s and the paper is silent, so it remains unresolved rather than confirmed-withheld); the exact licence of SingStyle111, which Shi et al. mark only as 'Restricted' and whose own terms I did not reach; whether any of the NC corpora publish a commercial-licensing fee schedule rather than just a contact address (Opencpop and JVS-MuSiC both invite enquiries, neither states terms); and whether ACE Studio's own EULA permits redistributing its rendered output as a training corpus at all, which determines whether ACE-Opencpop's CC-BY-NC-4.0 was the releasers' to grant. Finally, I found no dataset-side evidence on the singer-consent question the AI & SOCIETY paper raises — none of the thirteen corpora publish the consent form or release their singers signed, so what those singers actually agreed to is unknown from the public record in every single case.

lanes.title: Singing voice conversion & vocal identity

findings.title: Retrieval-based-Voice-Conversion-WebUI
findings.finding: MIT-licensed, not archived, last push 2026-08-04 (created 2023-03-27, 38,174 stars) — the only large-community SVC trainer still alive. Repo tagline is 'Easily train a good VC model with voice data <= 10 mins!' and the English README qualifies it as 'Training with a small amounts of data (>=10min low noise speech recommended)'. For streaming it claims 'We have achieved an end-to-end latency of 170ms. With the use of ASIO input and output devices, we have managed to achieve an end-to-end latency of 90ms.' F0 extraction defaults to RMVPE, which the README says 'Provides the best results (significantly) and is faster with lower resource consumption than Crepe_full'.
findings.implication: RVC is the default identity layer for a commercial product on one 5090: MIT on code and weights, ~10 min of a target singer, and sub-200 ms streaming that a practice companion can run live over a score-locked render.

findings.title: Retrieval-based-Voice-Conversion (library) — documented inference parameters
findings.finding: The documented parameter contract states exactly what survives conversion and what does not: `f0_up_key` (default 0) is 'Transpose (integer, number of semitones, raise by an octave: 12, lower by an octave: -12)' — the source F0 contour is copied and shifted only by whole semitones, never re-predicted; `protect` (default 0.33) exists to 'Protect voiceless consonants and breath sounds to prevent artifacts such as tearing in electronic music'; `index_rate` (default 0.75) is 'Search feature ratio (controls accent strength, too high has artifacting)'; `rms_mix_rate` (default 0.25) 'Adjust the volume envelope scaling. Closer to 0, the more it mimicks the volume of the original vocals.'
findings.implication: RVC composes with a score-locked pipeline rather than replacing it — pitch and timing are passed through untouched — but the defaults ship at 25% source loudness envelope and a named consonant/breath protection knob, so breath and dynamics are the two things a singing product must explicitly dial back in.

findings.title: so-vits-svc — SoftVC VITS Singing Voice Conversion (4.1-Stable)
findings.finding: ARCHIVED by the owner on 2023-11-11 and read-only; licence is AGPL-3.0. The README states the model preserves 'the pitch and intonations of the original audio', that the vocoder was replaced with NSF HiFiGAN 'to solve the problem of sound interruption', that training clips should be '5s - 15s', and — decisively for score work — that the `-a` / `--auto_predict_f0` flag should 'not enable this when converting singing voices as it can cause serious pitch issues'. Optional clustering/feature retrieval reduces timbre leakage but 'may slightly reduce clarity'.
findings.implication: The archetypal SVC repo is dead and AGPL-3.0, so it is not a commercial base — but its two documented rules generalise: an F0 predictor must be switched off for singing, and a source-filter (NSF) vocoder is what stops the pitch line from breaking up.

findings.title: seed-vc: zero-shot voice conversion & singing voice conversion, with real-time support
findings.finding: ARCHIVED (GitHub API: archived=true, last push 2025-04-20, 3,889 stars), licence GPL-3.0. While live it was the strongest zero-shot route: clone from 1–30 s of reference with no training; the SVC checkpoint `seed-uvit-whisper-base` runs at 44,100 Hz with explicit F0 conditioning and 30–50 recommended diffusion steps; measured real-time on an RTX 3060 Laptop GPU at ~300 ms algorithm delay + ~100 ms device delay = 430 ms total with 150 ms inference per chunk; optional fine-tune needs a minimum of 1 utterance and 100 steps (~2 min on a T4). Backing paper: 'Zero-shot Voice Conversion with Diffusion Transformers', arXiv:2411.09943.
findings.implication: The best-documented zero-shot singing route on consumer hardware is now abandoned AND GPL-3.0 — treat its numbers as the benchmark to beat, not as a dependency, and note that even it needed explicit F0 conditioning to do singing at all.

findings.title: Voice Conversion With Just Nearest Neighbors (kNN-VC)
findings.finding: Interspeech 2023, pp. 2053–2057; reference implementation github:bshall/knn-vc is MIT. The method replaces each source frame's WavLM layer-6 feature with the mean of its k nearest neighbours in the reference set, then vocodes with HiFi-GAN — a strictly frame-for-frame substitution, so source duration and phrasing are preserved exactly. The repo states the operative data law: 'The longer the cumulative duration of all reference waveforms, the better the quality will be (but the slower it will take to run). The improvement in quality diminishes beyond 5 minutes of reference speech.' Training the vocoder on pre-matched features gives the paper's best model at 6.29% WER vs 6.39% for standard HiFi-GAN.
findings.implication: Sets the honest floor for 'how much target audio': ~5 minutes, after which more data buys almost nothing — and because the substitution is frame-synchronous, a kNN-family converter cannot drift off a MIDI-locked timing grid.

findings.title: DDSP-SVC — real-time end-to-end singing voice conversion based on DDSP
findings.finding: MIT, not archived, last push 2026-08-12 (2,668 stars, v6.x). Data recipe is stated as clip count rather than minutes: 'The total number of the audio clips for training dataset is recommended to be about 1000' with each clip at least 2 seconds. Claims 'training time can be shortened by orders of magnitude' versus SO-VITS-SVC with hardware requirements 'significantly lower', and the real-time GUI uses 'sliding window, cross-fading, SOLA-based splicing and contextual semantic reference'. Explicitly concedes the trade: the 'original synthesis quality of DDSP is not ideal' and needs a vocoder/diffusion/rectified-flow enhancement stage to be competitive.
findings.implication: The one live SVC family whose core is an explicit harmonic-plus-noise source-filter model — so F0 is a first-class control input rather than something inferred — at the documented cost of needing a second enhancement stage before it sounds finished.

findings.title: The Singing Voice Conversion Challenge 2023
findings.finding: 26 submissions (24 systems + 2 baselines). Target-singer data supplied was 11.84–12.72 minutes of singing (150–159 phrases) per target for the in-domain task, and only 4.31–6.75 minutes of SPEECH (150–161 phrases, no singing at all) for the cross-domain task. The top system reached roughly 4.0 naturalness MOS against ground truth ~4.1 — human-level — but the best similarity score was ~2.6 on the 4-point speaker-likeness scale against ground truth ~3.0, a gap no team closed. Cross-domain was harder than in-domain specifically in similarity.
findings.implication: Naturalness is a solved problem in SVC and identity is not: budget ~12 minutes of clean target singing as the real requirement (not 10 minutes of speech), and expect the converted voice to be judged as 'not quite that singer' even when it sounds entirely human.

findings.authors: Violeta, Zhang, Shi, Yasuda, Huang, Wu & Toda
findings.title: An Extensive Analysis of the Singing Voice Conversion Challenge 2025 Evaluation Results
findings.finding: SVCC 2025 (training data released 2025-04-28, submissions due 2025-06-30) moved the target from singer identity to singing STYLE conversion: 7 teams, 26 systems evaluated (18 submissions, 6 baselines, 2 ground truth). XAB style-accuracy results name the hard cases exactly: 'difficult singing styles to model were breathy, glissando, and vibrato, achieving only 37.3%, 42.6%, and 43.9% style accuracy scores, respectively', versus the easiest — pharyngeal 44.8%, mixed voice 48.3%, falsetto 48.8%. Best-system naturalness fell back to ~3.7 MOS against ground truth ~3.9, i.e. below the human parity SVCC 2023 had reached.
findings.implication: Everything time-varying in a sung voice — breath noise, portamento between notes, vibrato modulation — is where SVC measurably fails, which is precisely the material a practice companion has to render correctly for the feedback to mean anything.

findings.authors: Chen, Gu, Cui, Zhang, Chen & Dai
findings.title: LCM-SVC: Latent Diffusion Model Based Singing Voice Conversion with Inference Acceleration via Latent Consistency Distillation
findings.finding: Measured real-time factors on an NVIDIA A100: DiffSVC 0.166, the teacher LDM (LCM-SVC-T) 0.369, and the distilled students 0.010 at 4 steps, 0.007 at 2 steps and 0.004 at 1 step — roughly a 92x speedup over the teacher. Quality barely moves across the step counts: seen-singer NMOS 3.880±0.073 (4 steps), 3.877±0.075 (2 steps), 3.827±0.078 (1 step), with SMOS 4.119 / 4.136 / 4.125.
findings.implication: Diffusion SVC is not inherently too slow for interactive use — consistency distillation buys two orders of magnitude of RTF for ~0.05 MOS, so a single 5090 can plausibly run a diffusion-quality identity layer inside a practice loop rather than only offline.

findings.authors: Bai, Geng, Wang, Wang, Guo, Gao & Li
findings.title: HQ-SVC: Towards High-Quality Zero-Shot Singing Voice Conversion in Low-Resource Scenarios
findings.finding: Accepted to AAAI 2026 (submitted 2025-11-11). The stated headline in the official repo (github:ShawnPi233/HQ-SVC) is 'Low-resource training (single consumer-grade GPU, <80h data)'. The abstract's diagnosis is architectural rather than about data volume: 'Existing methods model speaker timbre and vocal content separately, losing essential acoustic information that degrades output quality while requiring significant computational resources.' HQ-SVC instead extracts content and speaker features jointly through a decoupled codec, then models pitch and volume explicitly to preserve 'critical acoustic information typically lost in separate modeling approaches'.
findings.implication: The most current peer-reviewed result says the standard disentangle-then-recombine design is itself the quality ceiling, and that a whole zero-shot SVC system is now trainable on one consumer GPU with under 80 hours — a 5090 is inside the training envelope, not just the inference one.

findings.title: beatrice-trainer (Beatrice 2, v2.0.0-rc.0)
findings.finding: Released 2025-08-31. The card states in Japanese that 'the source code and trained models in this repository are released under the MIT License' — MIT covers the pretrained weights, not just the code. Training completes in about 40 minutes on a GeForce RTX 4090 and consumes about 9 GB of VRAM at default settings. Inference is CPU-viable: RTF < 0.2 single-threaded on an Intel Core i7-1165G7, with about 50 ms of latency measured through external recording equipment. It is one of only two model families still supported in w-okada/voice-changer v2 (the other being RVC); so-vits-svc, DDSP-SVC and MMVC were v1-only.
findings.implication: The cheapest commercially clean identity layer measured anywhere in this lane: 40 GPU-minutes and 9 GB to train a voice, then real-time on CPU alone — which frees the entire 5090 for the score-locked synthesis stage upstream.

findings.authors: Zhang, Zhang, Wang, Wang, Chen, Jia, Chen & Wu
findings.title: Vevo2: A Unified and Controllable Framework for Speech and Singing Voice Generation
findings.finding: Submitted 2025-08-22, revised 2026-03-05, accepted to IEEE/ACM TASLP 2026; shipped inside the Amphion toolkit (github:open-mmlab/Amphion, MIT, last push 2026-03-25). It separates a prosody/melody tokenizer (VQ-VAE, 512 vocabulary, 6.25 Hz) from a content-style tokenizer (16,384 vocabulary, 12.5 Hz) with timbre disentanglement, and a flow-matching acoustic stage 'that allows for timbre control'. Crucially it names 'style-preserved voice conversion' and 'style-converted voice conversion' as two distinct supported tasks, plus humming-to-singing and instrument-to-singing. Trained on Emilia-101k (~101,000 h speech) + SingNet-7k (~7,000 h singing). LICENCE TRAP: the Amphion code is MIT, but the Vevo2 checkpoints at hf:RMSnow/Vevo2 are CC-BY-NC-ND-4.0 — non-commercial AND no-derivatives, so even fine-tuning them is out.
findings.implication: The state of the art now treats 'keep the performance, change the voice' and 'change the performance too' as separate switches — exactly the distinction a score-locked product needs — but the only released weights that do it cannot be used or adapted commercially.

findings.title: Self-supervised restoration of singing voice degraded by pitch shifting using shallow diffusion
findings.finding: Submitted 2026-01-15 (CC-BY-SA 4.0). Frames conventional pitch shifting as a degradation to be repaired rather than a transform, on the grounds that it carries 'well known trade offs such as formant shifts and robotic coloration that becomes more severe at larger transposition jumps'. The fix is a lightweight mel-domain diffusion model conditioned on F0, volume and content features, with training pairs made self-supervised by applying a pitch shift and reversing it so the untouched original is the reference; it 'substantially reduces pitch shift artifacts compared to representative classical baselines' on both statistical and pairwise acoustic measures (no numeric values given in the abstract).
findings.implication: Confirms that transposing a performance to fit a target singer's range is a per-semitone quality tax, not a free operation — so a practice companion should re-render the line at the target pitch from the score wherever it can, and reserve transposition for small intervals.

findings.title: Vibrato Expression Control for Singing Voice Conversion with Improving Independent Control (VibE-SVC2)
findings.finding: Submitted 2026-06-15, accepted to IEEE TASLP. Names two concrete breakages in singing style conversion and fixes each: pitch–energy entanglement (addressed with an 'Energy Style Converter'), and F0 extraction collapse on non-modal phonation — 'Addressing specific styles such as vocal fry poses a challenge, as conventional F0 extraction often fails due to their inherent subharmonic characteristics', handled by a Subharmonic Correction algorithm on the F0 contour. It also adds vibrato rate scaling for independent control of vibrato extent, a capability absent from its own predecessor.
findings.implication: The F0 tracker, not the converter, is the first thing that fails on real singing — any score-locked pipeline that trusts an extracted F0 contour must detect subharmonic/fry regions or it will silently mis-transcribe the very passages a singer most needs feedback on.

lanes.gaps: I could not find any published real-time-factor or VRAM measurement for singing voice conversion on an RTX 5090, or on any RTX 40/50-series card — every hard RTF number in this lane is measured on an A100 (LCM-SVC), an RTX 3060 Laptop (Seed-VC), or a CPU (Beatrice, RT-VC), so 5090 throughput for a score-locked pipeline has to be measured locally rather than cited. I also could not find a controlled study that sweeps target-singer training minutes against conversion quality for SINGING specifically: the three numbers available are a repo recommendation (RVC, >=10 min speech), a repo observation on speech references (kNN-VC, plateau beyond 5 min), and a challenge's fixed allocation (SVCC 2023, ~12 min singing / ~5 min speech) — none of them is a measured curve, and none isolates how much of that budget must be singing rather than speech. Finally, two recent systems publish claims I could not verify with numbers: R2-SVC (arXiv:2510.20677, Zheng et al., 2025-10-23) claims state-of-the-art results under clean and noisy conditions via F0 perturbation and music-separation-artifact simulation but reports no figures in its abstract and names no code release or licence; and HQ-SVC's '<80h data, single consumer-grade GPU' claim appears only as a repo bullet, with no GPU model, VRAM figure, wall-clock training time, or baseline comparison table retrievable from the repo or abstract.
